entries.x: The journeys and systems of this demonstrator, drawn as an ArchiMate overlay on the DPI-H Reference Architecture's own ArchiMate model (smart-ra, version 0.3.0-draft.1). The RA's elements are unchanged and keep their ids, so each RA box here is the element smart-ra publishes. The overlay adds: the journeys J1 to J4.1 (the use cases) as business processes, one per BPMN process; the people who take part, as business roles assigned to the journeys whose BPMN has their lane; each of those roles associated with the RA stakeholder it belongs to: the caregiver with Citizens / Care recipients , the clinicians and the community health worker with Health Workers (a role and a stakeholder are different element types, so ArchiMate allows an association, not a specialization); the Thai and Lao systems, each a specialization of the RA building block it is an instance of, serving the journeys it takes part in; each journey's realization of the RA capabilities it exercises. Every box in a drawing links to its element's page. All views and elements. Systems on the Integrated View Thailand on the left, Lao PDR on the right, the layers of the RA's Integrated View (Fig. 3.2) in the middle, and WHO GDHCN beneath both. Systems on the DPI-H Integrated View Journeys (use cases) Journeys, people and capabilities One view per journey Journey View --- --- J1 Issue the birth-dose DVCs J1 on the DPI-H RA J2 Discover and refer the infant J2 on the DPI-H RA J3 Verify, import and schedule J3 on the DPI-H RA J4.0 Issue the family's VHLs J4.0 on the DPI-H RA J4.1 Read records at the point of care J4.1 on the DPI-H RA How it is made The model is generated, not drawn: python3 -I tools/archimate/build.py fetches smart-ra's model and its add views.py at the commit in tools/archimate/smart-ra.lock.json (sha256 checked), applies tools/archimate/overlay.py , and writes archimate/0.1.0/smart-trust-demo.archimate . The journeys and their people are read from processes/content/ and scenarios/roles.json ; the systems are those of VaxLink's architecture view. CI fails if the committed model is not what the build makes. The drawings are cat-harness's archimate subgraph's: no Archi, no Java.

One business process per journey. Each lane is a role on the personas page; each task names the skill that performs it. The BPMN source of each process is in processes/content/ , copied into the guide as input/business-processes/ . Select a diagram to open it in the process viewer, which lists each task and the skill that performs it. Process Lanes BPMN --- --- --- J1 Issue the newborn's birth-dose DVCs in Country A Caregiver, Birth clinic vaccinator, Birth clinic issuing system, Issuer signing key j1-birth-dose-dvc.bpmn J2 Discover and refer an unregistered infant in Country B Caregiver, Community health worker, CHW app j2-chw-discovery-referral.bpmn J3 Verify, import and schedule at the home clinic Caregiver, Home clinic provider, Home clinic EHR j3-clinic-verification-schedule.bpmn J4.0 Issue the family's records to one phone as VHLs Caregiver, National health portal, Issuer signing key, Family phone j4-0-family-vhl-issuance.bpmn J4.1 Read a family member's records at the point of care abroad Caregiver, Family phone, Point-of-care provider, Point-of-care receiver, National health portal j4-1-vhl-point-of-care.bpmn J1 Issue the newborn's birth-dose DVCs in Country A Process id Process J1BirthDoseDvc . Open in the process viewer. J1, Cross-border birth and initial vaccination. In Country A (XXR, the birth country) the provincial hospital gives a newborn who is not its own country's national the Hep B and BCG birth doses and issues one signed DVC per dose (DVCMinPreQual at subclaim -6) as a paper QR, with no national identity number needed (the WHO guide's QR Code Generation section 12 example is such a pair). The hospital system is the Issuer (SMART Trust) and the HCERT side of the VHL Sharer; the private key stays with the key holder (two-phase signing, STT-ISS-004, STT-COS-006). XXR's DSC, under its CSCA, being on the GDHCN trust list is a PRECONDITION of issuing, declared below, not a step. The caregiver is the Holder (SMART Trust, smart-trust-phw) and VHL Holder (IHE ITI VHL). Task checklist: j1-birth-dose-dvc.checklist.md. J2 Discover and refer an unregistered infant in Country B Process id Process J2ChwDiscovery . Open in the process viewer. J2, Return home, CHW discovery and referral. Back in Country B (home, XXH), where the family resides, the community health worker finds an infant born abroad who is missing from the household roster on a home visit. Offline, the CHW app adds the infant to the household (a FHIR Group, through a structured data capture form), reads the foreign DVCs without verifying them (read-unverified, STT-VER-011: the triage read stops before the trust lookup and marks every field unverified), saves the doses as reported by the family, not verified (Immunization.primarySource false), and refers the infant to the clinic for verification. Everything is queued on the phone and syncs when it next has a signal. The CHW app is a Receiver (SMART Trust, smart-trust-phw) that deliberately stops before trust; the caregiver provides the VDHC as Holder (smart-trust-phw requirement provide-a-vhl-to-a-receiver). Task checklist: j2-chw-discovery-referral.checklist.md. J3 Verify, import and schedule at the home clinic Process id Process J3ClinicVerification . Open in the process viewer. J3, Clinic verification and schedule generation, in Country B. The clinic EHR (Receiver in SMART Trust and smart-trust-phw, VHL Receiver side in IHE ITI VHL) holds a copy of the GDHCN trust list, which the trust anchor (Trust Network Anchor; IHE Trust Anchor) distributes and Country B, a Trust Network Participant, retrieves (smart-trust-phw retrieve-pki-material). Loading the DID documents is a PRECONDITION of this visit, not a step in it: the clinic may be offline throughout, so the list it verifies against is the one it last refreshed, about weekly, when the CHW visits the base clinic or district health office. It verifies each foreign DVC in the STT-VER-001 order against XXR's DSC DID document, imports the verified doses with provenance, adds the national schedule code beside each foreign vaccine code (ConceptMap; the nurse decides any product with no mapping) and evaluates the national schedule, which finds the 6-week doses due and books them. Task checklist: j3-clinic-verification-schedule.checklist.md. J4.0 Issue the family's records to one phone as VHLs Process id Process J40FamilyVhl . Open in the process viewer. J4.0, Outbound family travel, "One Family, One Phone". Before travelling, the caregiver who holds the family's one shared phone asks Country B's national portal for each family member's records, choosing for each a passcode the family can say aloud and an expiry (for example 14 days); the portal records that choice as the holder's consent to share (FHIR Consent, IHE Privacy Consent on FHIR). The portal, a VHL Sharer (IHE ITI VHL) and Issuer (SMART Trust, smart-trust-phw), issues one passcode-protected Verifiable Health Link per member: the documents (IPS, DVCs) encrypted as JWE (STT-VHL-007) behind an ITI-YY5 manifest, the link in the SMART Health Links payload format at HCERT key 5 (STT-VHL-001, STT-VHL-002), signed with Country B's DSC. The shared phone holds the QRs for the caregiver, the VHL Holder. The records themselves stay hosted in Country B: the QR carries only a pointer and a key. Task checklist: j4-0-family-vhl-issuance.checklist.md. J4.1 Read a family member's records at the point of care abroad Process id Process J41VhlFetch . Open in the process viewer. J4.1. Abroad, a child of the family needs care. The caregiver, the VHL Holder (IHE ITI VHL; Holder in SMART Trust and smart-trust-phw, requirement provide-a-vhl-to-a-receiver), opens her QR on the family phone and tells the passcode. The hospital system, a VHL Receiver (Receiver in SMART Trust and smart-trust-phw), verifies the HCERT against the GDHCN trust list, requests the manifest by ITI-YY5 with an HTTP Message Signature (STT-VHL-005, STT-VHL-006, STT-VHL-008) and decrypts the documents (STT-VHL-007). Country B's portal checks the passcode, returns the manifest and logs every request, granted or refused, as an AuditEvent at home (IHE BALP). If the HCERT does not verify, there is no digital verification: the VHL is not followed and the records are treated like paper. As in J3, loading the DID documents is a PRECONDITION of this visit, not a step in it: the hospital verifies against its cached copy of the trust list and needs no connection to do so. It refreshes that cache nightly or hourly, where an offline site such as the J3 clinic refreshes about weekly. Task checklist: j4-1-vhl-point-of-care.checklist.md.

The journeys tell the VaxLink story (issue 21): Somsack SENGMANY, born in Thailand (XXR), living in Lao PDR (XXH), seen again in Thailand a year later. Personas, system actors and stories recast; the business processes made generic (no person names in them). New process steps: J2 adds the newborn to the household and saves the doses as reported, not verified; J3 adds the national schedule code beside the foreign vaccine code (the nurse decides unmapped products); J4.0 records the holder's consent with a passcode and an expiry; J4.1 adds the home portal's lane, which checks the passcode, returns the manifest and logs every access. New examples: household Group , registration Questionnaire and response, reported and verified Immunization s, verification and adjudication Provenance , ConceptMap from product to schedule code, an illustrative schedule PlanDefinition , ImmunizationRecommendation and reminder Task , the four Lao doses, a six-dose IPS, Consent , and two AuditEvent s (access granted, wrong passcode). Two illustrative code systems stand in for PreQual product ids and national schedule codes. New page: VaxLink examples, mapping each walkthrough screen and payload to its example here.

The system actors of the journeys and the actor definitions of WHO SMART Trust, WHO SMART Trust PHW and IHE ITI VHL each is derived from. The decision-support logic is the DAK's component 6: the decisions the journeys make, as decision tables in the OMG Decision Model and Notation (DMN 1.3), as the WHO SMART Guidelines DAK writes them. Each table names the business-process tasks it serves, the requirements it applies, the data elements it reads and the FHIR artifacts that show it in the examples. Each is also a PlanDefinition (type eca-rule ) with one action per rule, so it is listed in the artifact index. The sources are processes/content/decisions/ .dmn ; this page and the PlanDefinitions are generated from them. The entries use the FEEL subset the harness's decision-table interpreter accepts: - (any), literals, comparisons and one-of. Every table's hit policy is FIRST: the rules are tried in order and the first that matches applies, so the order is part of the logic. Where a rule says "by national policy", the policy is the home country's; the tables illustrate the decisions, they are not a country's rules. One baby · two countries · one year Somsack is born in Thailand and grows up in Lao PDR. A year later, a Thai doctor sees every vaccine he has ever had, and no record is copied across the border. This guide is that story, the VaxLink walkthrough , written down as a WHO SMART Guidelines digital adaptation kit (L2) and a FHIR implementation guide (L3). It is built on the SMART Trust HCERT libraries and WHO GDHCN. J1 — Born abroad (Thailand, birth day) Precondition: the issuer's DSC is on the trust list. XXR's document signer certificate (DSC), issued under XXR's Country Signing CA (CSCA), was shared with the GDHCN, the Trust Anchor, before any DVC is signed; the GDHCN publishes it as a DID document. Sharing it is not a step of issuing. A DVC signed with a key whose DSC was never shared fails every receiver's trust-list check (STT-VER-006). Khamla gives birth to Somsack on 2025-10-28 at Chiang Rai Provincial Hospital, away from home. He has no Thai identity number. Dr Anan gives the Hep B and BCG birth doses and records them with their WHO PreQual product codes. For each dose, the hospital system does three things: 1. It builds a DVCMinPreQual payload: STT-PAY-001…005 and STT-PAY-007, with subclaim −6 (STT-SEL-003). No identity document is needed (STT-PAY-005). 2. It prepares the CWT and the bytes to sign: STT-CWT-001…005, STT-ISS-004. 3. It has XXR's key sign them (STT-COS-002, STT-COS-006), then finishes the HC1 text: STT-COS-001, STT-ZIP-001, STT-B45-001, STT-HC1-001, STT-QR-001. Khamla leaves with two paper DVCs. In the demo: the library tests use the WHO guide's own two signed HC1 strings (QR Code Generation §12), which verify against the live DEV trust list under the same XXR key. Somsack's DVC payloads are illustrative, as in VaxLink. Live issuance in the app uses a TEST-ONLY key (STT-ISS-003), whose DSC is not on the GDHCN list, so its DVCs do not verify in J3. Pain point: The baby has no Thai ID number, so his records would normally stay locked inside the Thai hospital’s system. Enabler: A digitally signed QR card travels with the family — no ID number or database lookup needed. Policy: Babies born abroad can get a verifiable vaccine record before they have the host country’s civil registration or a national ID — and registering the birth at home still matters. J2 — Found at home (Lao PDR, 3 weeks later) J2a. On a routine visit to Village 04, Vilay finds a newborn the Lao system does not know exists. Her phone has had no signal for weeks. Khamla shows the two cards. The CHW app reads them with read-unverified (STT-VER-011; STT-B45-002, STT-ZIP-002, STT-CBR-003), which needs no trust list. It shows the doses, but checks no signature and saves nothing yet. J2b. On the CHW app's newborn form (structured data capture, TrustDemoHouseholdRegistration ) she adds Somsack to the Sengmany household ( TrustDemoHousehold ), with a temporary id. Bounmy confirms the details as head of household. The app saves the doses read from the cards as reported by the family, not verified ( TrustDemoJ2HepBReported , TrustDemoJ2BcgReported : primarySource false). Vilay refers Somsack to the district health center ( TrustDemoJ2Referral ). Everything stays queued on the phone, for 28 days if need be, and syncs when it next reaches a signal. Pain point (J2a): Without a check, a forged or mistyped card could quietly become an official record. Pain point (J2b): Babies born abroad are invisible to the home health system until civil registration catches up — sometimes months later. Enabler (J2a): The phone reads the card offline, and keeps “what the family told us” clearly separate from “what we have verified”. Enabler (J2b): An offline form links the baby to his household immediately; it syncs once the phone finds a signal. Policy (J2a): Keep a clear line between what families report and what has been verified, and don’t grant trust too early. Policy (J2b): Newborns can be registered at home, offline, before civil registration or a national ID exists. J3 — Made official (Vientiane District Health Center, 4 weeks later) Precondition: the DID documents are already loaded. Loading them is not a step of this visit. The clinic may be offline all day, so the EHR fetches nothing during it: its trust store holds the GDHCN DEV trust list as it was last refreshed, including XXR's DSC DID document (STT-TRU-001, STT-TRU-002, STT-TRU-005). A clinic with no connection of its own refreshes it about weekly, when the CHW visits the base clinic or district health office, where Country B retrieves the list the GDHCN trust anchor distributes. A DSC published after that refresh is not in the clinic's copy, so its DVC fails the trust-list check (STT-VER-006) until the next refresh. J3a. Nurse Chanthasone opens the referral and scans the QRs. The EHR verifies each DVC offline against that copy (STT-VER-001…009, STT-KID-002), without contacting Thailand. If a DVC fails (a tampered card, say), the EHR names the step and the reason, the doses stay unverified, and the nurse decides by national catch-up policy. J3b. The Thai Hep B product matches nothing on the national schedule. The EHR keeps Thailand's product coding and adds the schedule coding beside it, from the national map ( TrustDemoProductToLaoEpi ). For the Hep B product the map has no entry, so Nurse Chanthasone makes the clinical call that it is the schedule's birth dose ( TrustDemoJ3Adjudication ), and her decision is added to the map for the next clinic. The schedule ( TrustDemoLaoInfantSchedule ) then runs: the birth doses count, and pentavalent 1, bOPV 1 and PCV 1 are due at 6 weeks ( TrustDemoJ3Recommendation ). Enabler (J3a): Thailand’s signing key is on the shared WHO trust list, so any clinic can check it locally. Enabler (J3b): Thailand’s original code is kept and the Lao code is added alongside; the schedule engine calculates what’s due. Policy (J3a): Trust is decentralized: a Lao clinic verifies a Thai signature itself, without contacting Thailand. Policy (J3b): Never overwrite another country’s record: keep the original coding alongside the national one. J4.0 — Crossing back: one family, one phone (Lao PDR, 12 months later) J4.0a. Somsack's summary ( TrustDemoJ4Ips ) shows six doses: two from Thailand, four from Lao PDR. For Somsack, Bounmy shares his record with a 4-digit passcode he can say aloud, valid for 14 days. The portal records his consent ( TrustDemoJ4Consent ), then does three things: 1. It assembles the IPS and Somsack's DVCs. 2. It encrypts them (STT-VHL-004, STT-VHL-007) behind a passcode-protected manifest with an expiry (STT-VHL-009). 3. It issues the link as an HCERT, with the VHL at key 5 (STT-VHL-001, STT-VHL-002), signed with Country B's DSC. The QR holds only a pointer and a key: the record stays in Lao PDR. Pain point (J4.0a): Many families share one smartphone; one-app-per-person designs leave them out. Pain point (J4.0b): Sending photos or PDFs of records leaks data and can’t be verified by the receiver. Enabler (J4.0a): A household wallet on one phone, with a separate health summary for each person. Enabler (J4.0b): A Verifiable Health Link: the QR holds only a locked pointer; the data stays home until the passcode is given. Policy (J4.0a): Design for shared devices (“One Family, One Phone”) so families with only one phone aren’t left out. Policy (J4.0b): Data sovereignty: the record stays in Lao PDR until the family authorizes someone to open it. J4.1 — Crossing back: a Thai doctor sees the full history (Chiang Rai, 12 months later) Precondition, as in J3: the DID documents are already loaded. The clinic viewer's trust store is a cached copy of the GDHCN trust list, including Country B's DSC DID document (STT-TRU-001, STT-TRU-002, STT-TRU-005). The clinic refreshes it nightly or hourly, against about weekly at the offline J3 clinic. It does not need to be online to verify: verifying reads the cache and never fetches the list. A DSC published after the last refresh fails the trust-list check (STT-VER-006), naming that reason. Back where it began, Dr Anan sees Somsack at a primary care clinic in Chiang Rai. Bounmy shows the QR on his phone and says the passcode. The clinic viewer and the Lao gateway take five steps: 1. The viewer verifies the HCERT against Country B's DSC in its copy of the trust list. 2. It requests the manifest by ITI-YY5, signed with HTTP Message Signatures (STT-VHL-005, STT-VHL-006, STT-VHL-008). 3. The Lao gateway checks the passcode, the expiry and the consent, returns the manifest, and logs the access at home ( TrustDemoJ41Access ). 4. The viewer decrypts the IPS and DVCs (STT-VHL-007) ( TrustDemoJ41Received ). 5. It shows them to Dr Anan: every dose since the birth, viewed, never copied. A wrong passcode is refused, and the attempt is still logged in Lao PDR ( TrustDemoJ41WrongPasscode ). If the HCERT does not verify (for example, Country B's DSC is missing from the cached list), there is no digital verification. The clinic names the step and the reason (STT-VER-008), does not follow the VHL, and Dr Anan treats whatever the family can show as he would a paper record. Pain point: Without the history, the doctor would repeat vaccines or have to guess. Enabler: The record is fetched live from Lao PDR, viewed without being copied, and an access log is sent home. Policy: Continuity of care across borders: each country keeps its own records, with no international patient registry and no vendor lock-in. What is agreed regionally is the data model and the trust list, not a shared copy of the data. Questions for discussion The VaxLink walkthrough closes with four policy questions: 1. Identity for babies born abroad (J1, J2b): how should national immunization systems handle temporary ids for cross-border infants before civil registration is complete? 2. Where trust begins (J2a, J3a): why should offline CHW devices store foreign cards as reported, not verified, rather than verify them in the field? 3. Matching vaccines across countries (J3b): when a monovalent vaccine is given abroad but the home schedule uses a combination (pentavalent), how should schedule rules count the doses still due? 4. Cross-border access and audit (J4.0b, J4.1): what agreements do countries need so that a clinician viewing a record abroad triggers an audit entry in the patient's home country?

Question: on what should the J1–J4 app be built, so that it runs the Kotlin HCERT library on Android (and, ideally, the web) on the most recent, most Kotlin-native Open Health Stack? 1. What Open Health Stack is today Open Health Stack (OHS) began as a Google-led set of components and is now the OHS Software Foundation , a community project under the Linux Foundation, which WHO joined in July 2026. Its code lives in github.com/ohs-foundation (28 repositories). There are two generations of the client libraries: Generation Libraries Platforms Distribution State --- --- --- --- --- android-fhir (first) com.google.android.fhir:engine , data-capture (SDC), workflow , knowledge Android only Google Maven "Maintenance"; last commit Feb–Mar 2026. Workflow runs CQL (HAPI-based, heavy). Kotlin Multiplatform (current) dev.ohs.fhir:fhir-model-r4 1.0.0-rc03, fhir-path-r4 , fhir-engine 2.0.0-alpha04, fhir-data-capture 2.0.0-alpha04, fhir-workflow 2.0.0-alpha01; dev.ohs.player:client 1.0.0-alpha03 Android, desktop JVM, iOS, web (wasmJs, and JS for some) Maven Central Active (commits this week); alpha APIs. Workflow does PlanDefinition/$apply ; CQL is "still to come". On top of the KMP generation sits the OHS Player , described by the foundation as a cross-stack reference toolkit, "reference, not product": player-reference : the client, a GitHub template app in Compose Multiplatform (Android, iOS, desktop, web from one tree). Screens are driven by configuration (SQL-on-FHIR ViewDefinition s compiled at build time), data entry by SDC questionnaires. It opens on an OIDC login and blocks on a first sync with a FHIR server; there is no bundled-data mode. player-client : the library behind it (configuration-driven FHIR views), usable on its own. ohs-player-reference-web-portal : a TypeScript admin portal for workforce hierarchies (users, access). Not a clinical web app; not relevant to J1–J4. ohs-player-reference-backend , -infrastructure : backend and deployment (FHIR gateway, data pipes). player-reference-examples : variants of the reference app (empty today). A natural place to offer the journeys upstream later — an OHS Foundation repository, so only by proposal, never from here. The most recent and most Kotlin-native choice is therefore the KMP generation , with or without the Player template. 2. Constraints every option must meet 1. The Android emulator test of the HCERT library (STT-GEN-004) must run in CI on an Android runtime, platform crypto included. This is independent of the app: it is a small Android test module that depends only on the HCERT jar (plan step 4). It can land before the app decision. 2. Offline and serverless demo. J2 is offline by definition, and CI cannot stand up an OIDC provider and FHIR server for an emulator run cheaply. The app needs a bundled-data mode. 3. Supply chain. Every artifact pinned with sha256, releases ≥ 14 days old, no install scripts. Fewer dependencies is better. 4. The HCERT library comes from a pinned smart-trust-tools commit as a JVM jar (owner's choice). On Android the JVM jar works as is. On the web it does not yet: hcert-core's Kotlin/JS target uses node:crypto and node:zlib , so it runs on Node, not in a browser, and there is no wasmJs target. Any web front end needs either a browser target in hcert-core (WebCrypto, CompressionStream ), a library change in smart-trust-tools, or the Rust/wasm library, which already runs in the browser with WebCrypto keys. 3. Options Option A — Fork the OHS Player reference app Create the app from the player-reference template; add an offline demo mode (bundled FHIR bundle, no login), the J1–J4 screens and the HCERT calls. Pros Cons --- --- It is the OHS Player: the most visibly "OHS" outcome, and the closest to what OHS implementers will start from. Requires an OIDC provider and a FHIR server to start; the offline mode is ours to write and to keep merging against a template that moves weekly. Android, iOS, desktop and web from one tree; configuration-driven screens; SDC questionnaires for registration (J2) and import (J3) come wired. 57 libraries and 8 plugins in its catalogue (Koin, Ktor CIO/Darwin, Kermit, ksafe, kotlinpoet, BigNum, Compose adaptive …), several alpha, plus their transitive graph: the largest pinning and verification burden of all options. Upstreamable: journeys could later become a variant in player-reference-examples . Kotlin 2.3 / AGP 8.11 / JDK 21; its build-logic and code generation ( ig-codegen ) are ours to audit. Much of the template (auth, sync, workforce registers) is unrelated to the journeys and is noise in a demonstrator. Option B — Own lean Compose Multiplatform app on the OHS KMP libraries (recommended) A small Compose Multiplatform app (Android first, web target alongside) written for the four journeys, using the same foundational libraries the Player uses — fhir-model-r4 , fhir-engine (on-device store), fhir-data-capture (SDC questionnaires for J2 registration and J3 import), fhir-workflow ( PlanDefinition/$apply for the J3 schedule) — and, optionally, dev.ohs.player:client for configuration-driven views. Pros Cons --- --- Same current OHS libraries as the Player, so it demonstrates the stack the OHS Foundation is building towards, without the template's auth/sync/DI layer. Not the Player app itself; screens are ours. Offline and serverless from the start; the emulator CI job can drive the journeys. The KMP libraries are alpha: API breaks between alphas are ours to absorb. Dependency set is roughly the libraries' own graph (Compose MP, Ktor client, Room3/SQLite, kotlinx) — still sizeable, but every addition is chosen and listed in docs/dependencies.md . fhir-workflow has no CQL yet: the J3 schedule rules must be expressed as PlanDefinition applicability conditions in FHIRPath (enough for a birth-dose schedule; WHO SMART immunization CQL would wait). Shapes the code so the journey screens can later be offered to player-reference-examples as a Player variant. Option C — Android only, on android-fhir (first generation) A plain Android app on com.google.android.fhir Engine + SDC (+ Workflow). Pros Cons --- --- Mature, production-proven (OpenSRP, EmCare); most documentation and examples. In maintenance; not where OHS is going; Android only (no web). Workflow library runs CQL today (WHO SMART Guidelines content). Workflow pulls HAPI FHIR + CQL engine: a very large, JVM-heavy dependency graph. Google Maven artifacts; the session's network policy currently blocks dl.google.com (needed for this and for AGP/AndroidX in every option). Option D — Web first, no Android app A static page on gh-pages running J1–J4 in the browser with the Rust/wasm library (or a future browser build of hcert-core), plus only the Android test module for STT-GEN-004. Pros Cons --- --- Smallest: almost no dependencies; easiest to show anyone with a link. Not OHS; does not show the Kotlin library inside an OHS app, which is the stated goal. The Rust/wasm library already runs in the browser. The Kotlin library on Android is exercised only by tests, not by a journey. 4. Recommendation Option B , staged: 1. Android test module for STT-GEN-004 first (independent of this choice). 2. The B app, Android target, offline, J1–J4, on dev.ohs.fhir engine + data capture + workflow. 3. The web target of the same app once hcert-core has a browser target (to be requested in smart-trust-tools) — or, in the meantime, the journeys' QR steps on the web through the Rust/wasm library. 4. Later, propose the journeys to the OHS Foundation as a player-reference-examples variant (owner's call; never pushed from here). If being the OHS Player matters more than dependency count and an offline demo, choose A : the plan is the same, with step 2 starting from the template and adding the offline mode first. 5. What any option needs from the environment dl.google.com (Google Maven: AGP, AndroidX, the Android SDK) is blocked by this session's network policy. It is needed to write the Gradle verification metadata for any Android build. GitHub's runners can reach it, so CI is unaffected; local builds here are. The stories are in scenarios/stories.json . Each moment ends with its pain point, what enables it, and the policy point it makes, as the VaxLink walkthrough presents them. J1 — Born abroad (Thailand, birth day) Precondition: the issuer's DSC is on the trust list. XXR's document signer certificate (DSC), issued under XXR's Country Signing CA (CSCA), was shared with the GDHCN, the Trust Anchor, before any DVC is signed; the GDHCN publishes it as a DID document. Sharing it is not a step of issuing. A DVC signed with a key whose DSC was never shared fails every receiver's trust-list check (STT-VER-006). Khamla gives birth to Somsack on 2025-10-28 at Chiang Rai Provincial Hospital, away from home. He has no Thai identity number. Dr Anan gives the Hep B and BCG birth doses and records them with their WHO PreQual product codes. For each dose, the hospital system does three things: 1. It builds a DVCMinPreQual payload: STT-PAY-001…005 and STT-PAY-007, with subclaim −6 (STT-SEL-003). No identity document is needed (STT-PAY-005). 2. It prepares the CWT and the bytes to sign: STT-CWT-001…005, STT-ISS-004. 3. It has XXR's key sign them (STT-COS-002, STT-COS-006), then finishes the HC1 text: STT-COS-001, STT-ZIP-001, STT-B45-001, STT-HC1-001, STT-QR-001. Khamla leaves with two paper DVCs. In the demo: the library tests use the WHO guide's own two signed HC1 strings (QR Code Generation §12), which verify against the live DEV trust list under the same XXR key. Somsack's DVC payloads are illustrative, as in VaxLink. Live issuance in the app uses a TEST-ONLY key (STT-ISS-003), whose DSC is not on the GDHCN list, so its DVCs do not verify in J3. Pain point: The baby has no Thai ID number, so his records would normally stay locked inside the Thai hospital’s system. Enabler: A digitally signed QR card travels with the family — no ID number or database lookup needed. Policy: Babies born abroad can get a verifiable vaccine record before they have the host country’s civil registration or a national ID — and registering the birth at home still matters. J2 — Found at home (Lao PDR, 3 weeks later) J2a. On a routine visit to Village 04, Vilay finds a newborn the Lao system does not know exists. Her phone has had no signal for weeks. Khamla shows the two cards. The CHW app reads them with read-unverified (STT-VER-011; STT-B45-002, STT-ZIP-002, STT-CBR-003), which needs no trust list. It shows the doses, but checks no signature and saves nothing yet. J2b. On the CHW app's newborn form (structured data capture, TrustDemoHouseholdRegistration ) she adds Somsack to the Sengmany household ( TrustDemoHousehold ), with a temporary id. Bounmy confirms the details as head of household. The app saves the doses read from the cards as reported by the family, not verified ( TrustDemoJ2HepBReported , TrustDemoJ2BcgReported : primarySource false). Vilay refers Somsack to the district health center ( TrustDemoJ2Referral ). Everything stays queued on the phone, for 28 days if need be, and syncs when it next reaches a signal. Pain point (J2a): Without a check, a forged or mistyped card could quietly become an official record. Pain point (J2b): Babies born abroad are invisible to the home health system until civil registration catches up — sometimes months later. Enabler (J2a): The phone reads the card offline, and keeps “what the family told us” clearly separate from “what we have verified”. Enabler (J2b): An offline form links the baby to his household immediately; it syncs once the phone finds a signal. Policy (J2a): Keep a clear line between what families report and what has been verified, and don’t grant trust too early. Policy (J2b): Newborns can be registered at home, offline, before civil registration or a national ID exists. J3 — Made official (Vientiane District Health Center, 4 weeks later) Precondition: the DID documents are already loaded. Loading them is not a step of this visit. The clinic may be offline all day, so the EHR fetches nothing during it: its trust store holds the GDHCN DEV trust list as it was last refreshed, including XXR's DSC DID document (STT-TRU-001, STT-TRU-002, STT-TRU-005). A clinic with no connection of its own refreshes it about weekly, when the CHW visits the base clinic or district health office, where Country B retrieves the list the GDHCN trust anchor distributes. A DSC published after that refresh is not in the clinic's copy, so its DVC fails the trust-list check (STT-VER-006) until the next refresh. J3a. Nurse Chanthasone opens the referral and scans the QRs. The EHR verifies each DVC offline against that copy (STT-VER-001…009, STT-KID-002), without contacting Thailand. Both verify, so it imports them as FHIR Immunization s ( TrustDemoJ3HepB , TrustDemoJ3Bcg ) with provenance ( TrustDemoJ3Verification ; STT-VER-007, STT-VER-008), replacing the reported doses of J2. If a DVC fails (a tampered card, say), the EHR names the step and the reason, the doses stay unverified, and the nurse decides by national catch-up policy. J3b. The Thai Hep B product matches nothing on the national schedule. The EHR keeps Thailand's product coding and adds the schedule coding beside it, from the national map ( TrustDemoProductToLaoEpi ). For the Hep B product the map has no entry, so Nurse Chanthasone makes the clinical call that it is the schedule's birth dose ( TrustDemoJ3Adjudication ), and her decision is added to the map for the next clinic. The schedule ( TrustDemoLaoInfantSchedule ) then runs: the birth doses count, and pentavalent 1, bOPV 1 and PCV 1 are due at 6 weeks ( TrustDemoJ3Recommendation ). Khamla leaves with the date ( TrustDemoJ3Reminder ). Over the year Somsack gets those doses and measles-rubella at 9 months, in Lao PDR. Pain point (J3a): Clinicians either distrust foreign paper and re-vaccinate, or trust it blindly. Pain point (J3b): Countries name and package vaccines differently, so doses get missed or repeated. Enabler (J3a): Thailand’s signing key is on the shared WHO trust list, so any clinic can check it locally. Enabler (J3b): Thailand’s original code is kept and the Lao code is added alongside; the schedule engine calculates what’s due. Policy (J3a): Trust is decentralized: a Lao clinic verifies a Thai signature itself, without contacting Thailand. Policy (J3b): Never overwrite another country’s record: keep the original coding alongside the national one. J4.0 — Crossing back: one family, one phone (Lao PDR, 12 months later) J4.0a. The family plans a trip to Thailand. Bounmy's phone holds the family wallet, with a profile for each of them. Somsack's summary ( TrustDemoJ4Ips ) shows six doses: two from Thailand, four from Lao PDR. Precondition, as in J1: Country B's DSC, under Country B's CSCA, is already shared with the GDHCN, the Trust Anchor. That is what lets the clinic in Thailand verify the link in J4.1. J4.0b. For Somsack, Bounmy shares his record with a 4-digit passcode he can say aloud, valid for 14 days. The portal records his consent ( TrustDemoJ4Consent ), then does three things: 1. It assembles the IPS and Somsack's DVCs. 2. It encrypts them (STT-VHL-004, STT-VHL-007) behind a passcode-protected manifest with an expiry (STT-VHL-009). 3. It issues the link as an HCERT, with the VHL at key 5 (STT-VHL-001, STT-VHL-002), signed with Country B's DSC. The QR holds only a pointer and a key: the record stays in Lao PDR. Pain point (J4.0a): Many families share one smartphone; one-app-per-person designs leave them out. Pain point (J4.0b): Sending photos or PDFs of records leaks data and can’t be verified by the receiver. Enabler (J4.0a): A household wallet on one phone, with a separate health summary for each person. Enabler (J4.0b): A Verifiable Health Link: the QR holds only a locked pointer; the data stays home until the passcode is given. Policy (J4.0a): Design for shared devices (“One Family, One Phone”) so families with only one phone aren’t left out. Policy (J4.0b): Data sovereignty: the record stays in Lao PDR until the family authorizes someone to open it. J4.1 — Crossing back: a Thai doctor sees the full history (Chiang Rai, 12 months later) Precondition, as in J3: the DID documents are already loaded. The clinic viewer's trust store is a cached copy of the GDHCN trust list, including Country B's DSC DID document (STT-TRU-001, STT-TRU-002, STT-TRU-005). The clinic refreshes it nightly or hourly, against about weekly at the offline J3 clinic. It does not need to be online to verify: verifying reads the cache and never fetches the list. A DSC published after the last refresh fails the trust-list check (STT-VER-006), naming that reason. Back where it began, Dr Anan sees Somsack at a primary care clinic in Chiang Rai. Bounmy shows the QR on his phone and says the passcode. The clinic viewer and the Lao gateway take five steps: 1. The viewer verifies the HCERT against Country B's DSC in its copy of the trust list. 2. It requests the manifest by ITI-YY5, signed with HTTP Message Signatures (STT-VHL-005, STT-VHL-006, STT-VHL-008). 3. The Lao gateway checks the passcode, the expiry and the consent, returns the manifest, and logs the access at home ( TrustDemoJ41Access ). 4. The viewer decrypts the IPS and DVCs (STT-VHL-007) ( TrustDemoJ41Received ). 5. It shows them to Dr Anan: every dose since the birth, viewed, never copied. A wrong passcode is refused, and the attempt is still logged in Lao PDR ( TrustDemoJ41WrongPasscode ). If the HCERT does not verify (for example, Country B's DSC is missing from the cached list), there is no digital verification. The clinic names the step and the reason (STT-VER-008), does not follow the VHL, and Dr Anan treats whatever the family can show as he would a paper record. Pain point: Without the history, the doctor would repeat vaccines or have to guess. Enabler: The record is fetched live from Lao PDR, viewed without being copied, and an access log is sent home. Policy: Continuity of care across borders: each country keeps its own records, with no international patient registry and no vendor lock-in. What is agreed regionally is the data model and the trust list, not a shared copy of the data.
